newsitem.title: UK: Police arrest one over IRA bombing in N. Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Police arrest one over IRA bombing in N. Ireland.

text.p: Police investigating a double IRA bombing of Britain's army headquarters in Northern Ireland said they arrested one man in a dawn raid on Thursday.
The arrest came less than 24 hours after police issued a photofit picture of one of the bombers, disguised in a hood, beard and dark glasses.
"Early this morning, a male from the Belfast area was arrested," said a police spokesman.

Monday's attack at Lisburn, 10 miles (15 km) from Belfast, was the Irish Republican Army's first attack in Northern Ireland for two years. Thirty-one people were injured and police called it "a deliberate attempt at mass murder."

The attack raised fears that Northern Ireland would be drawn back into the 25-year civil war which claimed more than 3,000 lives if the IRA's pro-British "Loyalist" foes retaliated by ending their two-year ceasefire.
Loyalist political leaders have implored the guerrillas not to return to violence.
The Combined Loyalist Military Command (CMLC), which rules over the Protestant guerrilla groups, is expected to meet within two days to decide on its reponse.
The CMLC's long silence since the IRA attack has encouraged hopes that it will stick to the ceasefire it called in 1994 to match the IRA's own.
The IRA abandoned its truce on February 9 with the first of a series of bombings on the British mainland, but it had not attacked Northern Ireland until this week.

The IRA has denied Loyalist charges that it was trying to draw its Protestant rivals into renewed conflict, saying the attack was intended to put pressure on Britain to allow its political arm, Sinn Fein, into peace talks.
Sinn Fein, which like the IRA wants a united Ireland, has been prohibited from taking part until the guerrillas declare a new truce.
Britain's Northern Ireland minister, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said Sinn Fein was still welcome to join the talks provided the IRA cooperated.

"If Sinn Fein want to come in, they know what to do," Mayhew told BBC radio. "We want to see Sinn Fein in, but on the same terms as everybody else. There must be a ceasefire first that is dependable."

Northern Irish police said the Lisburn attack was probably planned at least four months ago, when the peace talks sponsored by Britain and Ireland were just beginning. One of the cars used in the attack was bought in June.
The bombers had entered the army base through the main entrance and had probably obtained security passes to get through the heavy security.

The two car bombs each contained 500 pounds (225 kg) of home-made explosives. They exploded 20 minutes apart and were placed so that rescue services and people injured in the first blast would be caught by the second.

Stunned by the attack, Ireland's Prime Minister John Bruton called an urgent full-day debate in parliament on Thursday about the Northern Irish peace process, in which he intends to stress that the republic will not tolerate violence for political ends.
But parliament is expected to resist pressure to break ties with Sinn Finn.

The Irish Times said the parliament's sub-committee on Northern Ireland had reviewed contacts with Sinn Fein after the IRA claimed responsibility for the Lisburn attack, but that no change in policy was likely to emerge from the debate.
Bruton banned his ministers from meeting Sinn Fein after the IRA ended its ceasefire, but Irish civil servants have continued to hold meetings with the party.
